section_title: What responsibility comes with being entrusted to care for others?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 41 “Lord,” said Peter, “are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” 42 And the Lord answered, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom the master puts in charge of his servants to give them their portion at the proper time? 43 Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. 44 Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.

45 But suppose that servant says in his heart, ‘My master will be a long time in coming,’ and he begins to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat and drink and get drunk. 46 The master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate. Then he will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the unbelievers.

47 That servant who knows his master’s will but does not get ready or follow his instructions will be beaten with many blows. 48 But the one who unknowingly does things worthy of punishment will be beaten with few blows. From everyone who has been given much, much will be required; and from him who has been entrusted with much, even more will be demanded.

context_lines: Peter asks whether the preceding parable is addressed to the disciples or to everyone. Jesus answers with a manager entrusted to give the household its food at the proper time. Faithfulness means continuing that care until the master returns.

The opposite response is to assume the master is delayed, abuse the other servants and indulge in eating, drinking and drunkenness. The master’s unexpected arrival exposes that behavior and brings judgment.

Jesus then distinguishes a servant who knew the master’s will from one who acted wrongly without knowing. Greater knowledge brings greater accountability. The closing principle extends the responsibility: much is required from those who have received much.

The question is therefore larger than whether a person has a title or privileged place in the household. What has been entrusted to someone must shape how that person treats others and responds to the master.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly see a warning about faithful care, abusive leadership and accountability in proportion to what has been received. Wesley especially applies the manager picture to those who minister God’s word, and the Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize faithfulness during the wait for Jesus’ return. ([Wesley on Luke 12:41–48](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-luke/); [USCCB note on Luke 12:35–48](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/luke/12))

There is a real difference over whether saving faith can finally be lost. Wesley reads the servant’s fate as a warning that someone once faithful can fall and perish. The Catholic Church likewise teaches that faith is a gift that can be lost and must be nourished. In contrast, the Reformed Westminster Confession teaches that people truly accepted in Christ will persevere to the end, even though they can fall into serious sin. The Catechism and Confession state those broader teachings rather than explaining each detail of this parable. ([Wesley on Luke 12:43–46](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-luke/); [Catechism §162](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_one/chapter_three/article_1/iii_the_characteristics_of_faith.html); [Westminster Confession 17](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html))
god_plan_lines: First Peter calls elders to shepherd God’s people willingly, without greed or domination, and points ahead to the Chief Shepherd’s appearing. The responsibility and future reckoning Jesus describes find a close parallel in that instruction to the church’s leaders. ([1 Peter 5:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/5.htm))

James similarly warns that teachers will be judged more strictly. Greater opportunity to shape others is not a reason to feel beyond correction; it brings responsibility for how that opportunity is used. God’s purpose for His people includes care that reflects the Lord they await. ([James 3:1–2](https://biblehub.com/bsb/james/3.htm))
